headline: Cornell bans frat parties. Faculty turn on its president.
summary: A student says seven men drugged and raped her at a Cornell fraternity party in 2024. The prosecutor got a six-page statement and charged no one. She sued last month. On Tuesday the president banned fraternity parties for the year and gave state police a role in assault cases. Wednesday night his faculty took up a no-confidence vote.

cover_question.q: Why did they ban all the parties?

cover_answer: A student was hurt at one, and the college fell short after.
table_question: If one person breaks a rule, should everyone lose the privilege?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: A big college called Cornell stopped all the parties at its fraternity houses, the clubs where some students live. A student was hurt badly at one, and the college didn't keep her safe enough afterward. Now real police will help, like a lifeguard added to a pool. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: A lifeguard at the pool. What happened to her stays off the card.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event and reads your face before your words, so the script keeps the assault off the card and hands them the lifeguard: the fix, not the harm. Expect "is she okay now?" She left the college. Say the police are helping and the parties have stopped.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: In 2024 a student told Cornell she was assaulted at a frat party. The prosecutor got a six-page file and charged no one. She sued. On Tuesday the president banned frat parties for the year and put state police on cases. Now the faculty vote on whether they still trust him, like a team voting on its captain.
8-12.why: Report, thin file, no charges, lawsuit, ban, vote. In order.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out whether adults apply their own rules, so the script runs the chain in order: a report, a six-page file, no charges, a lawsuit, a ban, a vote. The team voting on its captain is the mechanism: the people under a leader get a say. Expect "why didn't the police do more?" The state's top lawyer is asking that too.

13-17.script: A college president bans every frat party over one case. Fair to the other houses, or the only move left? Cornell's did it Tuesday, after a student said seven men raped her at a party in 2024 and no one was charged. Second: his faculty are voting no confidence. Does a late apology earn him another chance?
13-17.why: Whether a blanket ban is fair, and whether a late apology counts.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the president apologised and changed the rules, and her lawyer says the fix came too late for her. The script asks whether a blanket ban is fair to houses that did nothing, then whether a late fix earns a second chance. Expect "will anyone go to jail?" No one is charged yet.

5-7.q: Why did they stop the parties?
5-7.a: A student was hurt at one, and the college didn't do enough after. So the parties stop until it learns how to keep students safe.

8-12.q: Why did they ban all the parties?
8-12.a: One party went very wrong, and the college can't say its houses are safe. Every party stops until a review says how they can go on.
A club where male students live together and throw the parties.

13-17.a: No one in 2024. The state attorney general is investigating now.

13-17.q: What does a no-confidence vote do?
13-17.a: Nothing by itself. It's the faculty saying they don't trust him. The articles don't say what comes after.
